newsitem.title: UK: Blue Circle accuses govt over cement sales.
newsitem.headline: Blue Circle accuses govt over cement sales.

text.p: Britain's biggest cement producer Blue Circle Industries Plc predicted on Tuesday that 1996 U.K. cement sales volumes will be down around four percent, blaming government for its failure to invest in infrastructure.

Speaking at a news conference chief executive of the group's Blue Circle Cement division Ian McKenzie said an anticipated second-half recovery had not materialized and called government spending "disgracefully low."
Earlier the company's half year results showed U.K. cement sales down eight percent from the first half of 1995, offset slightly by a pick-up in exports.
McKenzie expects second-half sales volumes to match the weak year-earlier period, "so for the year as a whole we'll be down around four percent, which is very disappointing."

"Six months ago we were anticipating a good recovery in the second half. This didn't happen," McKenzie said, adding that housing starts have failed to follow the pick-up in the housing market, while infrastructure spending is historically low.

"If that continues, the damage done to the competitiveness of UK industry would be very great indeed. It isn't good enough for the government to say the Private Finance Initiative (matching public and private funding) will deal with this."

McKenzie estimated that infrastructure investment is "probaly 40 percent" below the levels seen in the second half of the 1980s, while U.K. cement prices "are low compared to most of Europe and low historically in real terms."
"It is important to us that we see real price recovery," the divisional head said. "We are looking for increases sensibly above the rate of inflation."

Blue Circle reaffirmed its enthusiasm for fresh investment internationally, telling reporters it would look for a minimum post-tax return on its investments of 10 percent, with the U.S., south-east Asia and Argentina favoured targets.
The U.S., Malaysia and Chile continued to power the group forward, with Malayan Cement's operating profit jumping 58 percent in the first half to 17.8 million stg.

Group chief executive Keith Orrell-Jones said that, although it was not counting on "phenomenal" Malaysian growth continuing indefinitely, it saw no cause for concern, apart from the current account deficit, which he said the government was "clearly now alert to".
The company also played down the possiblitly of new entrants threatening its position in the fast-growing and lucrative Chilean market, where it is one of just three cement suppliers.
